title: Europe’s carbon border charge changes the cost of switching suppliers
bank: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
summary: A border charge on carbon-intensive imports makes the EU's domestic carbon price more effective in the authors' simulation, but also raises the cost of manufactured goods faced by French households. The key choice for a French manufacturer is where it buys a covered input. If one supplier must pay for emissions while another escapes the charge because it is outside the system, switching suppliers can lower costs without reducing the demand for a carbon-intensive product. Extending the charge to imports changes that calculation. The paper is a comparison of two policy designs ahead of implementation. Its French price and global emissions results are model outcomes, rather than early readings of the new border mechanism.

The starting point is the EU Emissions Trading System introduced in 2005. Firms in covered industries face a carbon price, which gives them a reason to economise on fossil fuel use. Their customers can respond to higher input costs by sourcing elsewhere. Earlier research which the authors summarise here finds that French firms increased imports of products covered by the scheme from outside its geographical scope. That response is central to the comparison. An estimate holding the supplier network fixed would miss both a reason for the domestic policy to lose effectiveness and a reason why extending it to the border might raise prices further.

The model allows French firms to choose among suppliers and between covered and other inputs according to relative cost. The authors use product-level French import data from 2004, before emissions trading began, to estimate how attractive each origin is relative to French supply. Their estimates assign a comparative advantage in some emissions-intensive raw materials and petroleum products to exporters including Russia, Australia and Norway. Norway is an ETS member in this comparison, while the other two are outside. The distinction illustrates why comparing countries on raw emissions intensity alone would miss part of the incentive that a purchasing manager faces. The model matches observed import shares for regulated and unregulated goods (model estimation section).

With a domestic carbon charge calibrated to the ETS price, the model produces a decline of 0.7 million tonnes of global carbon dioxide emissions and a 0.87% rise in the price level of French manufactured products. Shifting purchases outside the regulated area limits the emissions reduction. The model reproduces about four fifths of the empirically estimated sourcing leakage, which supports its ability to capture that particular response. It is a narrower validation than an independent test of how accurately it predicts household prices, or of firms' behaviour once the previously untaxed imports are covered.

Adding a charge on imported covered goods increases the projected emissions reduction sevenfold. The projected rise in the French manufacturing price level becomes 1.42%, an additional 0.55 percentage points above the domestic-only case. The percentages describe changes from the baseline across the two scenarios. They do not imply a doubling of the level of goods prices. Firms substitute away from supplies from outside the regulated area, including Russia and China, towards cleaner sources such as French producers. The authors identify reduced international competitiveness for affected firms alongside greater emissions abatement (policy scenario section).

The useful investor distinction is between a relative-price adjustment in the affected goods and a persistent change in the inflation rate. The paper quantifies the former for France. It does not give a monthly path for the adjustment, an estimate for aggregate euro-area consumer prices, or a mapping from higher input costs into the margins of an individual manufacturer. Nor does the simulation value the change in emissions against the cost to households. The relevant question for company exposure is which part of a value chain can change source or production technology and which part ultimately bears the higher price. The authors specifically distinguish sourcing shifts that relocate emissions from investment that makes production cleaner.

questions.question: Which exposures depend most on the possibility of switching suppliers?
questions.detail: The model reproduces much of the estimated leakage under the domestic system, but the note gives no product-by-product response under the border charge. That matters for relative performance among importers and domestic input producers. Consult the paper cited in the note for substitution estimates, then map affected products to official trade flows, supplier concentrations and companies' procurement disclosures.

questions.question: How much of the incremental input cost reaches consumer prices, and how quickly?
questions.detail: The additional 0.55 percentage points is a simulated French manufacturing price-level effect. Its timing and distribution between margins and prices remain open. For an inflation or earnings thesis, compare contracts and inventories with producer prices, import unit values and selling prices for matched covered goods, using unaffected products to distinguish carbon costs from movements in energy or currency prices.

questions.question: What would materially weaken the projected emissions benefit?
questions.detail: The sevenfold improvement depends on the relative responses of suppliers and purchasers. A projection of global abatement is harder to verify than a change in French imports. Examine official carbon-content measurement and coverage rules alongside verified emissions at origins gaining or losing orders. Evidence that production simply shifts to different customers abroad would qualify an inference drawn from European purchases alone.
